Its first home is the GP2 SSD, rated for more than 18 million random reads per second.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Kioxia Corporation showcased a prototype of its new XL-Flash Generation 3 technology, next-generation low-latency, high-performance flash memory, at its KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo. The flash, which uses CMOS directly Bonded to Array, or CBA, for better power efficiency and storage density, is about 135% more efficient with 70% higher bit density than Gen 2, and its 3 µs average read latency is less than 10% of that of Kioxia’s standard BiCS8 TLC. Samples are due March 2027, and Kioxia named its GP2 enterprise SSDs, rated for more than 18 million 512-byte random read IOPS, as its first product using it.

The low-latency XL-Flash fills “a new memory tier” to bridge the gap between DRAM and regular flash memory, in a way that can complement or replace some DRAM to help drive down costs, especially in AI servers and data centers. This has some similarities to Optane, which used 3D XPoint instead, as a storage class memory (SCM) option to reach higher IOPS. Intel and Micron’s 3D XPoint stored bits as changes in the cell material’s resistance rather than as trapped charge like NAND, and Intel exited the Optane business in 2022. The XL-Flash NAND is built on BiCS flash technology, but it’s tuned for low read latency and high write endurance.

The first generation was SLC with under-5 µs reads, arriving in 2019. By 2022, Gen 2 added 2-bit MLC as an option for lower bit cost, trading some like-for-like performance for better price-to-density. Gen 3 is reported to use SLC, and its 3 µs average read latency challenges the first gen’s sub-5 µs rating while being more than ten times faster than the 40 µs of standard BiCS8 TLC. This is within the same ballpark as Optane SSDs. The flash also reportedly has SLC endurance at 150,000 to 250,000 P/E cycles, at least 50x standard TLC, running at a 4.8 Gb/s interface speed.

XL-Flash achieves lower latency, in part, by using more, smaller planes (16 per die, with a 4KB page, on earlier generations), which is common with SLC and low-latency flash, and especially helps with smaller I/O. Kioxia’s GP drives target 512B accesses rather than the typical 4KB, a pattern that matches developments in enterprise storage requirements for AI and other emerging workloads that involve constant fine-grained memory lookups. 3D XPoint would outmatch it for write performance, though, due to not needing to erase for new data.

The newer gen is able to maintain high levels of performance at much higher density thanks to CBA bonding, where Kioxia makes the logic CMOS wafer and flash memory-cell wafer separately and later bonds them. This technology also improves the efficiency of 512-byte reads, by Kioxia’s own tests, which matches the design intention of the forthcoming GP2. Kioxia hasn’t disclosed full details on the flash, such as layer count.

The GP2 Super High IOPS SSD will be Kioxia’s first product to use the new flash, promising high levels of performance, including up to 28 GB/s sequential reads, if it can saturate PCIe 6.0 x4 as expected. Kioxia’s 2.5x IOPS number, versus “typical TLC-based SSDs,” comes from a comparison to its own CM10 drives, for 512B I/O. Endurance will also be excellent at up to 50 drive writes per day, which is within the ballpark of Optane storage.

Kioxia is considering E1.S and E3.S form factors, and the drive will support direct liquid cooling, which is increasingly necessary for certain data centers, including GPU-heavy ones where the GP2 is likely to operate.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

These drives will serve as a flash tier to help get more out of a GPU’s HBM, and Kioxia first showed the GP series with Nvidia earlier this year. Offloading memory by any means possible is becoming a strategy with AI, even at the enthusiast level, due to high memory demands and how the technology and its KV caching work.

While the flash should sample to select customers before the end of the first quarter of 2027, Kioxia only promises GP2 evaluation samples to select customers by the end of that year. Exact specifications for the drive may differ, but what is clear is that later GP drives will target up to 100 million random-read IOPS that Kioxia and Nvidia have been working toward for AI servers. Kioxia announced its XL1 series of CXL memory expansion modules on XL-Flash in August, and it “will continue to leverage the speed, power efficiency, and endurance of XL-FLASH” for emerging data center needs.

#10444. How to protect your retirement savings if the AI bubble bursts

After stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov. 20, 2026, many Americans are asking themselves whether the huge bet on artificial intelligence is heading south.

While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks.

Before Monday’s surge, the NASDAQ had plunged about 18% since early October and had lost more than US$4 trillion since Nov. 16. The broad-based S&P 500 also took a beating and had shed all its gains for the year.

As a finance professor and certified financial planner, I can’t tell you whether the bubble has truly burst for good. But I can explain how the default model that most 401(k) plans use works, where it protects you, and what you might consider changing.

Whether AI stocks recover or not, the steps that protect a retirement account are the same: Know what you own, keep the mix of assets in balance, and hold enough in savings and low-risk funds to cover the years when you’ll need it.

Here are some basic facts to guide your planning.

Many Americans are saving on autopilot

Most 401(k) savers hold a target-date fund, which is named for the year of your “target” retirement and is often chosen as a default option by the employer. To understand how the current stock market volatility affects retirement savings, it’s important to first explain how these funds work.

About 55% of U.S. families have a defined contribution retirement account, such as a 401(k) or an individual retirement account. And inside a 401(k), the investing is increasingly done for you.

Six in 10 plans administered by the fund giant Vanguard signed workers up automatically in 2025 when they started a new job. And when those plans set a default investment, 98% of savers choose a target-date fund.

About 60% of the nearly 5 million savers in those plans held a single target-date fund and nothing else. Taken together, target-date funds now hold $4.8 trillion.

Inside each target-date fund is a list of index funds, which are named so because they track a particular market index. Vanguard’s series, the largest, is built mainly from four indices: U.S. stocks, international stocks, U.S. bonds and international bonds. The mix changes the older the saver gets, gradually moving away from high-return, high-risk stocks to safer, lower-yielding bonds.

For example, Vanguard’s 2055 fund was just over 91% stocks at the end of September 2026, reflecting the relative youth of those holding it. That share drops to 16% for savers invested in the 2027 fund, who expect to retire imminently.

Tech volatility is forcing new questions

That autopilot model is now being tested, starting with Nvidia.

In the span of a week, Nvidia went from riding the AI boom to getting mired in crisis. On Nov. 5, after the U.S. midterm elections raised the prospect of new curbs on AI and data centers, Nvidia shares fell more than 9%, while the broad-based S&P 500 index lost 4.4%.

Then, on Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned. By the end of that week, Nvidia had lost more than $1 trillion in market value within a month.

That slide may now be reversed. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Nov. 23, causing its share price to soar.

More broadly, it’s too early to say whether the AI bubble is over. Some analysts argue that it’s just losing some air rather than bursting. But amid the turmoil in tech stocks, savers may wonder whether a retirement plan on autopilot should adjust to this fresh volatility.

Target-date funds have significant tech exposure

Target-date funds are marketed as broadly diversified, often holding thousands of stocks, and financial advisers repeated that point after Huang’s exit.

But those stocks aren’t held in equal amounts. Index funds weight companies by market value. So as the value of AI-linked companies soared, their share has grown in the funds most 401(k) savers hold.

And that gets to the question of whether there’s a tech bubble riding on overvalued AI companies.

By the end of 2025, the 10 largest companies made up nearly 41% of the S&P 500, according to RBC Wealth Management. Yet those 10, almost all of which are in tech and AI, were expected to produce only about 32% of the index’s 2025 earnings.

In other words, investors are paying a premium for these shares because they’re expecting great profits later. Bad news can shrink that premium quickly.

Savers should also know that a target-date fund dilutes the concentration of AI stocks, but it doesn’t remove them. At the end of September, the 10 largest companies made up 36% of Vanguard’s total U.S. stock fund, with Nvidia at 7%. A 2055 fund keeps about 55% of its money there. So roughly 20 cents of every dollar was riding on 10 companies, and about 4 cents on Nvidia. That means even a small drop in these stocks can have a big impact on your fund, depending on its asset mix.

And while diversification hedges against one company’s turmoil, it’s less helpful if there’s a broad repricing of tech stocks. Even in Vanguard’s international fund, the four largest holdings are all tied to chipmaking, led by Taiwan Semiconductor, which makes Nvidia’s chips.

Furthermore, diversification doesn’t mean guaranteed protection all the time. In 2008, during the global financial crisis, funds built for people retiring in 2010 lost nearly 24% on average.

What to check now if you own a target-date fund

In principle, savers don’t need to do anything as long as they choose to stay on autopilot until retirement. Fund managers buy and sell assets to stick to the target mix – a practice known as rebalancing.

But rebalancing resets only the broad categories rather than trimming one particular company for growing too large. As Nvidia’s share of the market rose, so did its share of the fund.

For people who hold just one target-date fund, I believe the right response to this month’s news is to leave their 401(k) account alone. The fund has been rebalancing all along, and your stake in any one company is modest.

But a saver still needs to check three things.

First, consider the year you expect to retire. If you want to move it earlier or later, or want more or less risk, you should choose a fund with a different year.

Second, look at what the fund’s share of stocks is today, which is on the fund’s fact sheet. If you’re 60 and your fund is 60% stocks, a 30% fall in stocks would cut your balance by roughly 18%. If that would derail your retirement plans, you can switch to an earlier-dated fund that holds less in stocks and brings less risk.

Third, if you have other funds, you should review them. About 1 in 4 target-date investors in Vanguard plans hold other funds. If you add a tech fund or an S&P 500 fund, your account is riskier and more concentrated than the label suggests.

What to do if you hold other funds

About 31% of savers in Vanguard plans opt out of target-date funds and choose their own investments, perhaps because they find target-date funds too conservative or their fees too costly. For these investors, and for anyone with old 401(k)s and IRAs, there is more to do.

Start by looking at the fact sheet for each fund, like this one for Vanguard’s S&P 500 index fund, and compare the top holdings. An S&P 500 index fund, a large-cap growth fund and a technology or Nasdaq-tracking fund look like three investments. But in fact you may own the same handful of companies three times.

Next, you should rebalance your holdings according to your plan, not to a prediction. That means returning to the mix of stocks and bonds that you chose in the first place. Trades inside a 401(k) don’t trigger taxes, and many plans offer automatic rebalancing. If yours doesn’t, a simple rule backed by Vanguard research works: review once or twice a year, and rebalance whenever any part of your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target.

Finally, consider broadening the stocks you own. Morningstar Indexes strategist Dan Lefkovitz has pointed to U.S. value stocks, smaller companies and international stocks as areas with less AI exposure. Your plan may offer funds for each.

None of these makes you immune to losses, and diversifying can mean trailing the hottest part of the market for years. But the pattern can flip quickly: International stocks gained about 29% in 2025, far ahead of the S&P 500’s 16%.

Align your savings to your timeline

How much this month’s news matters depends on when you’ll need the money.

If you’re decades from retirement, a downturn can work in your favor, because every paycheck contribution buys shares at lower prices. Keep contributing and capture your full employer match. My own research with a colleague has found that accounts on systematic investment plans akin to 401(k)s earned better market-adjusted returns than accounts funded with lump sums.

If you’re within 5-10 years of retirement, the bigger danger is what planners call sequence-of-returns risk: A large loss right before or just after you start withdrawing can permanently shrink what your savings can support. A good defense is to hold several years of expected withdrawals in lower-risk assets, such as bonds or money market funds, so you’re never forced to sell stocks after a drop. For retirees, Morningstar’s Christine Benz suggests one to two years of withdrawals in cash and five to eight more in bonds.

What not to do

The costliest mistake is usually the most tempting: selling everything and waiting for the dust to settle.

During the 2008-09 financial crisis, about 117,000 Fidelity 401(k) participants moved entirely out of stocks. Those who stayed out saw their balances grow just 2% by mid-2011, while those who kept some stock exposure saw balances rise 50% on average.

Other moves to avoid include stopping your own 401(k) contributions, chasing whatever theme looks safe this month, and pulling money out early, which can mean taxes, penalties and a locked-in loss.

Last, don’t hand the decision to a chatbot. It will likely give you sound general guidance, such as diversifying and not panic-selling, and that consensus advice is where AI is reliable. But it is weakest on high-stakes questions that turn on your own situation.

This story was updated on Nov. 23, 2006, to note Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO and the rebound in the company’s share price.

Pawan Jain is a professor of finance at Texas A&M University.

#10442. 5 ways to tidy up your tech setup

One of the greatest tech-related purchases I’ve made of late is a product with no technology in it.

I was feeling overwhelmed by the assortment of laptops, tablets, and other gadgets accumulating around the house and finally decided to do something about it. That’s how I wound up with a 10-slot device organizer from a brand called MobileVision.

I almost ordered the seven-slot version instead, but quickly realized there’d be no trouble filling a few more spaces. I also snaked a USB-C cable up behind the organizer, so I can always be charging something.

This simple accessory has been a revelation, and not just because it helped tidy up my office. In my head it also creates a default place to store everything, which means one thing less to think about. This must be what actually organized people feel like all the time, I guess.

This story first appeared in Advisorator, Jared’s weekly tech advice newsletter. Sign up to get free tech tips every Tuesday.

The device organizer isn’t the only way I’ve been trying to tidy up my gadget situation. Here are a handful of other solutions I’ve accumulated over the years:

Retractable chargers

I mentioned retractable charging cables back in my year-end list of favorite tech things. The Baseus charging station on my desk (seemingly discontinued, though I’m happy with it) has a built-in cable I can pull out when my phone needs a top-up, while a separate Anker charger in the living room has a pair of retractable cables for the kids’ iPads. Both have cut down on the number of cables constantly dangling about.

Charge connector adapters (with lanyards)

While I’d love it if all my devices charged via USB-C, I’ve got a few stragglers that depend on Apple’s Lightning connector or the aging Micro USB standard. Instead of keeping separate cables around for these devices, I’ve decluttered by using little charging adapters that snap onto any USB-C connector.

The key is to find ones with built-in lanyards, so they can hang onto to a USB-C cable even when they’re not plugged in. I use these Lightning-to-USB-C adapters for the aforementioned kids’ iPads, and have finally gotten around to buying a similar set for Micro USB.

Cable ties

I am forever hoarding the velcro ties that sometimes come with charging cables, so I can use them to bunch various charging and data cables together. Huge packs of them are also available for cheap. (Alternatively, you can install cable hiders to keep things extra clean, but I’m reluctant to head down that rabbit hole.)

Docking stations and stands

Perhaps you noticed the lack of an iPad Pro to go with the Magic Keyboard in my organizer. That’s because it has its own magnetic charging stand in front of my desk, where I often use the iPad to take interview notes.

Beyond that, I bought this cheap 3-in-1 Anker charging stand years ago, and it remains a nightstand fixture both at home and on the road. It works with any phone and earbuds with wireless charging, and you can snake a third charging cable through the USB-A port underneath. (Ostensibly, it’s for Apple Watches, but I’ve used it for other things as well.) I’ve also got a Steam Deck docking station that keeps it fully charged.

I’m not saying you need to go on a massive organizational spree right now, but over time these little improvements have brought some much-needed order to my device empire. Perhaps they’ll give you some ideas of your own.

Alternatively, you might just be thinking that I have too many gadgets sitting around to begin with. But that is a problem for another day.

#10441. Which 2026 Samsung Galaxy Tab should you buy?

Samsung has a huge lineup of Galaxy tablets to choose from right now, and they’re all a little different.

The Galaxy Tab S12+ is the Samsung tablet to choose for a premium mix of entertainment, creativity, and productivity. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra gives you an even bigger canvas, while the Galaxy Tab S11 brings flagship features to a more portable size. For everyday value, start with the Galaxy Tab S10 FE series or the affordable Galaxy Tab A11+.

Samsung’s tablet lineup covers everything from watching a show on the couch to sketching your next project or getting work done between meetings. The right choice comes down to what you want that extra screen to do.

With options across a wide range of price points, Samsung has a Galaxy tablet for different needs and budgets this holiday season.

Here’s a list of the main Galaxy Tab options available in 2026, from family-friendly entertainment to Samsung’s largest creative workspace:

Screen size is only one part of the whole story. The Galaxy Tab S11, S12+, and S12 Ultra have AMOLED displays that offer rich contrast for movies and photos, while the FE models provide useful everyday features at a more accessible price.

The Galaxy Tab S12+ is the sweet spot if you want a serious upgrade over a basic tablet without moving to Samsung’s biggest screen.

As we covered in our Galaxy Tab S12 launch story, it combines a 12.6-inch 120Hz AMOLED display with a MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor, 12GB of RAM, and an included S Pen, with four months of complimentary Adobe Photoshop access and a six-month Notability trial, both of which support the stylus.

The S12+ is easy to use and appreciate in daily life. It puts reference material beside your notes during a course, sketch ideas for a presentation, while making it easy to settle into a movie after finishing your email. It has room to spread out without requiring the Ultra’s larger footprint.

The Galaxy Tab S12+ also offers a 5G version, making it worth considering if you regularly work away from Wi-Fi.

Buy the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra when the screen itself is the upgrade you’ll enjoy every day.

The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is made for creative professionals and families seeking premium entertainment. It moves naturally between focused creative work and immersive movie nights at home.

Its 14.6-inch AMOLED display gives photos, drawings, and multiple app windows more breathing room. Picture reviewing a document while keeping your handwritten notes visible, or drawing with reference images alongside your canvas.

The Ultra shares the S12+’s Dimensity 9500 processor but offers configurations up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. It’s available for $1,399.99, but last year’s Tab S11 Ultra is on sale during Black Friday for just $899.99.

Both S12 tablets ship with Android 17-based One UI 9 and seven years of OS and security updates. Photoshop comes pre-installed with a four-month access offer, giving you a way to explore S Pen-assisted photo editing.

The Ultra is especially appealing with a keyboard at a desk; Samsung’s Ultra Book Cover Keyboard Slim is the perfect companion to the S12 Ultra, and is on sale for $146.99 during Best Buy’s Black Friday Deal event.

Yes, the Galaxy Tab S11 is the premium Galaxy tablet to choose when portability comes first.

Our Galaxy Tab S11 launch coverage highlighted the return of Samsung’s smaller flagship tablet, with a Dimensity 9400+ processor, 12GB of RAM, and an included S Pen. Its 11-inch AMOLED screen makes it an attractive companion for reading, travel, and handwritten notes.

The Galaxy Tab S11 is the sort of tablet you can bring to a meeting or pull out on a train without needing a large work surface. You still get premium display quality, just in a size that’s easier to carry, and it comes in at a lower price.

A discounted Tab S11 Ultra can also be worth considering if you want a 14.6-inch screen. Compare the actual price with the S12 Ultra rather than dismissing an older flagship automatically.

The Galaxy Tab S10 FE and FE+ are compelling choices for people who want an included S Pen without flagship pricing.

Choose the 10.9-inch FE for a study companion that travels easily. Choose the 13.1-inch FE+ when you’d rather put a lecture, document, or recipe beside your notes. Both offer IP68 water and dust resistance, so they’re great kitchen companions.

Galaxy Tab S10 Lite is for students, children, and emerging creators. It is a practical, encouraging gift for handwritten learning, organization, drawing, and experimentation.

The Galaxy Tab A11+ is the straightforward entertainment choice. At $199, it’s the cheapest of the Galaxy Tab options, but it doesn’t support the S Pen, so choose an S-series model if handwriting matters.

Choose the Galaxy Tab S12+ for a premium all-rounder, the S12 Ultra for a spacious creative workspace, or the S11 for flagship features in a travel-friendly size.

For school, home projects, and everyday notes, the FE series delivers the features many people actually need. For family streaming and browsing, the A11+ keeps things simple and affordable.

The best Galaxy Tab isn’t automatically the biggest or newest. It’s the one that makes the things you already love doing easier — and gives you a few new possibilities along the way.

#10439. A fashion reporter’s favorite things of 2026

I’ll admit it. Being a fashion reporter can be a lot of fun. I get to sit across from some the most brilliant minds in the industry and peek at gorgeous collections seasons before they hit stores—long before they start shaping what we will wear.

But what most people don’t realize is that the job also involves a lot of squinting at fiber-content labels. I’ve asked founders extremely nerdy questions about leather tanning methods. I’ve toured factories and tromped through cotton fields.

Along the way, I come across many products. Over the course of a year, I wander through dozens of stores, wade through stacks of applications from brands hoping to land on our annual lists, and put bold new product claims to the test.

Most of it is forgettable. But every so often, I come across something that I love: a clever jacket that is also beautiful, heels you can actually walk in all day, a pair of sneakers with a story so moving I still think about it months later. This list is the best of what I found in a year of poking, prodding, and road testing. If you’re shopping for someone who cares about style and quality, these are good bets.

Every Stitch Tells a Story
Resolute RGL, Najla in Olive Green, $350

Of the many products I reviewed this year, this is the one that made a biggest impression. Each Resolute sneaker carries a hand-embroidered panel of tatreez, the Palestinian cross embroidery that has passed down through generations. Each panel is stitched by a woman who lives in the villages in the South Hebron Hills of the West Bank. She chooses the pattern and colors herself, and a panel takes 14 to 24 hours to complete. The cooperative co-owns the company, and embroiderers are paid as soon as their panels are finished. The shoes themselves are lovely, with an olive suede upper, memory foam insoles, and recycled rubber soles. It usually takes several weeks to make the shoes to order, but for the holidays, Resolute has prepared inventory so all products can be shipped within two days.

Light as a Feather, Tough Enough for a Nor’easter
Cole Haan, Grand Flex Fenella Buckle Lace-Up Waterproof Booties, $240

Most winter boots are heavy, adding weight as you trudge through the snow. Cole Haan has engineered these boots to be lightweight, but still set on a chunky lug sole that provides traction on icy sidewalks. They’re made from waterproof leather with sealed seams and a foam footbed that keep them cushy through a full day of walking. The buckle and laces give them a little edge, and a hidden ankle zip means you don’t have to do the laces again every time you leave the house.

Mary Poppins Would Be Into This
Parker Thatch, Jack Tote in Leopard, $1,250

I am a person who carries too much: laptop, a novel, a snack, and a backup snack for my kids. The Jack allows overpackers to carry what they need for the day without looking like a duffel bag. It’s made from leopard-print hair-on cowhide with black leather trim and handles, and it fits a laptop with room to spare. There’s an interior zip pocket, two open pockets so your phone and glasses don’t get lost, and a snap closure. It’s the ideal gift for a professional woman in the market for a power bag.

In-Law-Approved Loungewear
Lake, DreamModal Kimono Three-Piece Pants Set in Velvet Green Pencil Stripe, $168

The holidays involve lots of overnight guests, which can pose a dilemma. You want to be cozy, but you don’t want your in-laws to see you in your slinky nightgown or threadbare college T-shirt. Lake has many lounge sets. This one includes a wrap top with bell sleeves, a scoop-neck tank, and wide-leg pants with an elastic waist. It’s all made from a silky modal fiber, so it feels like you’re wearing pajamas but it looks like you’re in an outfit. The green and white stripe is festive without being kitschy. It’s machine washable, too.

Yes, You Can Walk in These Heels
Margaux, The Paloma Platform in Gold Nappa, $395

For years, most women assumed that “comfortable heels” is an oxymoron. Margaux is working hard to prove them wrong. The Paloma shoe has a 3.5-inch block heel, with a 1-inch platform, allowing you get the height without feeling unstable. There is plush foam padding under the sole and the straps are positioned so they don’t pinch. They’re handmade of nappa leather in Spain. I like the gold ones because they go with every holiday outfit.

Honey, I Shrunk the Handbag
Maison de Sabré, The Mini Palais in Candy Plum, $675

Some nights call for nothing more than a phone, a lipstick, and a credit card. The Mini Palais is just big enough for these things, and its adjustable strap lets you wear it crossbody, on the shoulder, or in hand. The bags are also sustainable. Maison de Sabré skips conventional tanning, which is heavy on chemicals, in favor of DriTan, a waterless tanning technology. Each bag carries a serial number that allows you to trace it back to tanneries and farms in the Netherlands. And you can dress the bag up with adorable charms made from scraps of colorful leather discarded on the factory floor.

A Glamorous New Design from Away

Away, The Aluminum Edge Carry-On, $428

Aluminum luggage has a certain glamour, but it’s heavy. Away’s new Aluminum Edge gives you a touch of aluminum on the frame and corners, but constructs the body out of a lighter polycarbonate shell that has a leather-like finish. It is full of luxurious touches, like champagne or nickel hardware. It closes with a lock, instead of a zipper, and it has a leather top handle. It comes in four colors, including a fun pink.

Twelve Days of Clean Beauty
Credo Beauty, Not Your Average Advent Calendar, $175

Credo, a retailer that stocks only nontoxic beauty brands, launched an Advent calendar full of 12 full-size bestsellers (worth $445 in products) inside a blue beauty case. Some of my favorite products inside include a Westman Atelier lipstick, Saie’s mascara, and Nécessaire’s hand cream. There’s no waste in this Advent calendar. You’ll carry the toiletry bag around for years to come.

Swimwear for a Winter Escape
Minnow, Women’s Marigold Floral V-Neck One Piece, $218, and Marigold Floral Pareo, $128

If you’re lucky enough to be headed somewhere warm over the holidays, or you’re already dreaming about next year’s beach trip, this is what I’d pack. Minnow is a resort brand that makes thoughtfully designed swimwear. This summery set provides substantial coverage, while staying put so you can enjoy the pool with your kids. The matching pareo means you can wear the outfit to your hotel’s buffet breakfast before lounging poolside. (And if the whole family is coming along, the suit can be coordinated with matching styles for everybody.)

A Functional, Beautiful Jacket
Overland, Kylie Reversible Sheepskin Jacket, $1,195

If you read my coats roundup this fall, you’ll recognize this jacket, made by Overland, which has been making sheepskin coats since 1973. I’m bringing it back because of all the jackets I tested this year, this one stood out. One side is a sleek leather jacket that has a strip of shearling peeking out at the collar. If you flip it inside out, it transforms into a plush shearling jacket. The pockets work from either side. It’s built to last, too, since sheepskin can last a lifetime with proper care.

A Blanket-Like Scarf
White + Warren, Cashmere Travel Wrap in Antique Gold, $385

Cashmere scarves are a traditional holiday gift, since they’re something anybody can appreciate. But this one stands out. It’s made of 100% cashmere but at almost 7 feet long, it works as a scarf, an evening wrap, or a full-body blanket on a red-eye. It can squish into a tote bag, but when you wear it, it feels substantial. It comes in a rainbow of colors; my favorite is the antique gold.

For the Bag Obsessive Who Has Everything
Assouline, Fashionphile: The Book of Iconic Bags, $120

Here’s a gift for the bag obsessive. Fashionphile, the luxury resale platform, knows exactly which bags hold their value and why. It has teamed up with Assouline to produce a silk-covered, 280-page tome about the 25 most influential handbags of all time, from the Hermès Birkin to the Fendi Baguette and the Dior Saddle, plus newer icons from Bottega Veneta and Loewe. It has more than 200 illustrations that will be eye candy to fashionistas.

Three Earrings in One
ME+EM, Transformer Earrings, $495

This piece of jewelry magically transforms to suit your outfit. The earrings start as gold-plated studs for the office. Clip on the detachable pendant and they become drops for dinner. The pendant is double-sided, with black marbled resin on one side and gold on the other, so you can flip it to suit your mood or your outfit. They’re made in Italy, and they work as well with a turtleneck as with a cocktail dress.

#10435. What’s open and closed on Black Friday 2026? Stocks, banks, mail, Walmart, Costco, and more

After a national day of Thanksgiving, consumers have traditionally kicked off their holiday shopping on Black Friday.

But are stores open and ready for it just one day after employees ate all that turkey? Here’s everything you need to know about what is open and closed on Black Friday.

Is Black Friday a federal holiday?

No, Black Friday is not a federal holiday, no matter what your shopaholic friends and family members may claim.

Are banks open on Black Friday?

Most banks are open on Black Friday, but some may have reduced hours because it is Thanksgiving week.

Is the stock market open on Black Friday?

Yes, both the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are open, but both institutions close early, at 1:00 p.m. ET. Perhaps all those buyers and sellers need a nap after eating some Thanksgiving leftovers.

Is the Post Office open on Black Friday? Is mail delivered?

Yes. U.S. Postal Service post office locations will be back in action on Black Friday. Mail will also be delivered.

Are FedEx and UPS delivering on Black Friday?

Yes, UPS is back to normal on Black Friday.

Some FedEx locations may have modified hours. Additionally, on-call and drop box pickups may be early. 

Are schools open on Black Friday?

Most schools will be closed for Thanksgiving break but it is a good practice to double-check with your student’s institution.

Are restaurants open on Black Friday?

Most restaurants will be open to help fuel shoppers for a long day of deal hunting. Call ahead, though, to double-check your favorite mom-and-pop joint. It might take some time off.

Are retail stores open on Black Friday?

Absolutely. Retail stores such as Best Buy, Walmart, Target, and others desperately want your business. Many sales have already started online ahead of the big day.

One notable exception is REI. For more than a decade, the outdoorsy store has promoted its “Opt Outside” initiative, remaining closed on Black Friday. Instead of shopping, it encourages people to take a hike, a walk, or do any outdoor activity.

Are pharmacies open on Black Friday?

Yes. Most pharmacies are open on Black Friday, including chains like CVS and Walgreens.

Are grocery stores open on Black Friday?

Yes, if you don’t have any Thanksgiving leftovers and need some grub, most grocery stores are open on Black Friday and happy to help. Membership-based stores like Costco and Sam’s Club will also be open.

#10433. Build Live Video Chat With WebRTC: From First Call to Production Debugging

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production issues that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:

Start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

1.     Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

2.     Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3.     Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted users hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:

1.     Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2.     Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

3.     When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4.     For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5.     On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:

1.     Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

2.     Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

3.     In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4.     In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

One peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1.     The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2.     The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3.     The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4.     Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

On a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Users deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try new network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

1.     Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

2.     In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3.     Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

4.     Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

5.     Check the negotiated codec and how quickly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

#10432. The simplest well-being strategy leaders overlook

As leaders, we spend a lot of time thinking about employee well-being. I’ve found that supporting it often comes down to the everyday choices we make. That includes some of the simplest choices we tend to overlook. One of them is getting outside.

We know spending time in nature is good for us. What’s striking is how hard it can be to do.

The American Nature and Health Survey, which was supported by the REI Cooperative Action Fund in partnership with the Nature and Health Alliance, highlights this increasing disconnect. In the 2026 survey, Americans shared that nature is essential to their lives, yet we’re spending less time in it. A decade ago, 25% of respondents spent less than two hours a week in nature. Today, that number has nearly doubled to 45%.

You can likely imagine why. Our lives are increasingly designed around convenience and screens. We can work, shop, connect, and entertain ourselves without ever stepping outside. Technology has made much of our lives easier and better, but it has also changed how we spend our time, often without us consciously making that choice.

That matters because time in nature is linked to lower stress and better mental and physical health. And it doesn’t have to mean hours on the trail. Research suggests even 20 minutes outside can help us feel more centered, in mind and body.

A RETAILER CLOSING ON BLACK FRIDAY

For many people, there are real barriers to spending time outdoors, including access and safety. For others, it’s simply the competing demands of work and daily life. We still value nature, but too often, life makes it difficult to choose.

That point has stuck with me as a business leader. There are plenty of things leaders can’t control. But we do have influence over how people spend their time at work and the conditions we create for people to do their best. With well-being, that means asking whether the way we work creates room for people to step away, recharge, and spend time outside.

At REI Co-op, we’ve been exploring one version of that idea for more than a decade. In 2015, the co-op made an unusual choice for a retailer: We closed our stores on Black Friday, one of the most deeply ingrained traditions in American retail. We paid our employees to spend the day outside and encouraged customers to do the same. We called it Opt Outside.

We didn’t tell employees how to spend the day or define what counted as “outside.” It could be a long hike, a walk through the neighborhood, time at a park with loved ones, or simply a quiet moment outdoors. The point was to create room for something that’s remarkably easy to push aside.

MAKE CHOICES

More than a decade since that first Opt Outside, I think there’s a leadership lesson in that choice, and it extends beyond REI. Not every company should do what we did. As leaders, we all make choices about what we make room for.

Those choices don’t have to be big. Could your next one-on-one be a walk outside? Could a team gathering happen outdoors? Where in the workday could we make stepping outside, even for a few minutes, a little easier?

These are small choices, but that’s the point. Supporting well-being and creating a better experience at work doesn’t always require another program or initiative. It starts with the everyday choices we make as leaders, and the things those choices make possible for others.

CHOOSE TIME OUTSIDE

This Black Friday, REI will once again close our stores and give our employees the day to spend outside. I’ll be doing the same, heading out for a hike with my family.

One day outside doesn’t solve everything, and it’s not meant to. But after more than a decade of Opt Outside, at REI we still believe there’s value in choosing time outside. It has reinforced something for me about leadership: Our job is sometimes to look at what’s standing in the way of making different choices, and see what we can do to change it.

Mary Beth Laughton is president and CEO of REI Co-op.

#10429. Black Friday 2026: These unexpected items are driving up U.S. consumer spending

The U.S. retail industry’s version of the Super Bowl is here with the arrival of Black Friday, an occasion that sellers online and in stores seize to drive year-end sales. This year, the day once considered the holiday shopping season’s unofficial kickoff might look to spectators more like the fourth quarter of a football game.

Brands and retailers have promoted steep discounts under the Black Friday banner all month, and some began rolling out deals before Halloween. But enough die-hard traditionalists hit the shops as soon as they can after Thanksgiving that the day remains the year’s biggest for foot traffic at physical stores, according to Sensormatic Solutions, a retail technology company.

“Black Friday is still the day for in-store shopping,” said Grant Gustafson, Sensormatic’s head of retail consulting and analytics.

Stores also have kept drawing a majority of holiday season spending, although e-commerce captures a bigger share every year, according to U.S. Census data. Industry analysts expect the trend to continue; consumers spent $82.5 billion online from November 1 to November 22, a 9.1% increase from the comparable three weeks last year, according to research by Adobe.

Retailers and consumers are giving Black Friday 2026 some other twists. The day’s evolution into a multiweek event has encouraged shoppers to stock up on discounted household basics while checking off their holiday lists, retail analysts said. Artificial intelligence and cost concerns are influencing how, where, when and on what consumers spend, retail analysts said.

“It’s not just a moment where shoppers are buying gifts,” said Caila Schwartz, a retail and consumer insights leader at Salesforce. “They’re also buying things that they need, and so that’s going to help drive up a lot of the spend.”

Here’s more on the emerging trends for Black Friday and holiday shopping overall:

Low views of the economy aren’t expected to dim holiday sales

This year’s holiday shopping takes place in a U.S. economic environment marked by voter frustration over gasoline prices fueled by the U.S. war with Iran, and high inflation overall.

Analysts and economists scrutinize retail spending on the five days that begin with Thanksgiving Day and end on Cyber Monday for clues about consumers’ financial staying power and commercial prospects heading into the new year.

Retail sales were up and down all year as filling up a car and other nonnegotiable costs took more out of household budgets. Commerce Department figures for October showed Americans pulling back on buying books, clothes, sporting goods, and other items.

The good news for retailers is that consumer confidence jumped this month as U.S. gas prices continued a steady decline.

The National Retail Federation estimated that higher prices would account for about half of the 4.1% sales growth it expected in stores and online in November and December. The group forecast U.S. shoppers collectively spending $1.01 trillion.

Black Friday still might have bigger discounts despite early deals

U.S. retailers have broadly held the line on prices instead of making big increases across the board, and offered solid discounts that persuaded customers to shop earlier, industry analysts said.

Salesforce, which tracks digital spending at a range of retailers, including grocery stores, said November discounts before Black Friday were 8% bigger than last year’s. Early promotions pushed average selling prices of physical merchandise 1% below last November’s prices, Salesforce said.

Retailers nonetheless were likely to reserve their best prices for Thanksgiving Day and Black Friday, Vivek Pandya, director of digital insights at Adobe, said.

For example, discounts on TVs are expected to average 23% on Friday compared with 11% during the first 22 days of the month, according to Adobe.

Shoppers are buying household items along with holiday gifts

The deepest discounts between this past Tuesday and Monday were expected on clothing, home goods, and health and beauty, Salesforce said. The company said it expected health and beauty products to average 33% off.

With Black Friday commencing well before the day itself, some consumers apply seasonal bargains to last long after the holidays by filling their cupboards with toiletries and clothes they would typically buy at another time, according to analysts.

Online sales of personal hygiene products were 40% higher from November 1 through November 22 compared with the October average, according to Adobe’s data. Sales of household cleaning products spiked 33% and clothing basics by 27% during the same time frame, Adobe said.

“Usually, when you think of holiday shopping, it’s premium handbags and jewelry and those types of items, but we’re fast seeing shoppers also use this season to stock up on the essentials,” Pandya said.

AI tools may be persuading users to do more online shopping

Consumers are using AI-powered shopping tools to help them compare products and prices, particularly as inflation and paying more for gasoline have made them more attuned to price tags, Pandya said.

Traffic to online retail sites from links in AI-powered tools more than doubled this month compared with November 2025, Adobe said.

A belief that e-commerce sites will offer “the best value possible” has contributed to shoppers’ doing more of their holiday period spending online instead of in stores, Pandya said.

—Anne D’Innocenzio, AP Retail Writer

#10428. Hands-on: Baseus’ new PicoGo Pro USB-C charger is clever, cute, and on sale

USB-C chargers are pretty standardized at this point, but there’s a fun new trend of adding displays to your power brick that I’ve been very much enjoying, and the new PicoGo Pro from Baseus is a great example with three ports, optimized charging, and a cute little character to top it off – and for Black Friday, it’s pretty deeply discounted, too.

The Baseus PicoGo Pro (AH22) is a 100W, 3-port USB-C charger designed to top off your laptop, phone, and/or tablet, even all at the same time. For anyone who travels often or just has a lot of devices on hand, chargers like this are a must. Having something you don’t have to think twice about when it comes to charging rates is just so nice, and these have come a long way, too.

Using GaN tech, PicoGo Pro is very compact at about 2 inches tall and a little over an inch wide. I remember having single-port chargers that could barely fast-charge my phone that were twice this size just a few years ago. GaN just absolutely rules, and Baseus is using a special version that reduces heat and improves efficiency.

But the two reasons I really like this charger aren’t strictly to do with GaN.

The first is the built-in display. Again, that’s a trend throughout the industry. Anker has several chargers out with built-in displays as the company helped to really make this popular – the Anker Prime 160W brick is really similar to PicoGo Pro (at a higher price), and it’s the only I’ve been using for months before trying out this Baseus model.

Baseus has a cute little animated character that accompanies your charging, with little eyes when the charger isn’t active and some fun animations to show your charging rate in real-time. Neat! You can “press” the button to move through the UI and even see the specific charging rate of each connected device. You’ll also see that the brick can recognize the device you have plugged in, though Android devices just show a generic “SAMSUNG” or whatever brand you plug in – Anker, again, had a similar set of features in a brick released earlier in 2026, but some of those features were iPhone-only, and that brick was only a 1-port, 45W charger anyway.

But, like that Anker brick, Baseus supports “smart” charging that adjusts to your device. Plugging in a Galaxy Z Fold 8 that was around 65% full, I saw the brick adjust its charging speed to tailor to the phone, initially going up to full speed before settling down around 28W~. You can manually adjust this with “Turbo” or “Gentle” modes, the former maxing out the charging rate and the latter settling in around 15W for a slower charge. That flexibility is great because it means you can adjust the charging rate to what you need in that moment. Full-speed for a quick top-off on a busy day, slower charging overnight to preserve battery health.

Baseus isn’t doing much new here, though the GaN tech mentioned earlier is enhanced by some architecture and algorithm adjustments the company has made behind the scenes, but it’s a really good implementation.

Beyond that, it’s also priced pretty well.

Baseus PicoGo Pro’s full price is $59.99, but you’ll probably rarely see it there. Technically, today is its launch date, and it’s already down by over 30% at $39.70 for Black Friday. Value-wise, this one is hard to beat.

Machines using Winbond-based SPI flash not fixable without new hardware, while vulnerable AMD PCs likely need new BIOS files.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former owners of laptops gained yet another concern today. Firmware-backed drive encryption setups like Windows' BitLocker are meant to protect against someone stealing your laptop or desktop computer. Prospective thieves would have a hard time guessing your PIN, as they'll eventually have to wait 10 minutes for each attempt. That is, unless your machine uses a modern AMD CPU or relies on Winbond's SPI flash — in which case your data may be open for inspection in a few days, or even hours, as researchers from Technische Universität Berlin found out.

The paper covers many vulnerabilities, but we'll focus on the big three. All focus on having a way to brute-force an encrypted drive's password in a matter of days/hours rather than years. Physical access is required for the attacks, but hardware theft is precisely the scenario that disk encryption is meant to protect against.

An attacker makes brute-forcing easier by resetting, or pretending to increase, the counter that records the number of failed unlock attempts. On Intel- and AMD-based PCs using the fTPM for security — nearly all modern x86 consumer machines — this counter is stored encrypted in an SPI flash chip on the motherboard.

Standard procedure is to allow for 32 attempts in succession, then force the machine to wait 10 minutes for each additional one, resulting in many years for unlocking a short PIN — 19 years for a six-digit numerical PIN, under normal conditions. We should note the attacks likely extend to other fTPM-based disk encryption mechanisms, not just BitLocker. While encryption keys can be alphanumeric, Microsoft Windows does default to using a numeric PIN for sign-in, and most users don't use long ones.

First up: machines based on Winbond's RPMC-enabled SPI flash (variant with rollback protection), used by many OEMs across both Intel and AMD platforms. Although it's hard to pin down the number of affected machines, the paper claims Winbond has roughly a 25% market share for SPI flash — so, potentially millions of machines. With a simple voltage glitch, the researchers made the chip reveal the HMAC key, the datum that signs commands when the TPM and the SPI chip talk to each other.

With the HMAC in hand, the thief places a low-cost interposer board in front of the SPI chip to impersonate it. On a failed unlock, the computer will request a counter increase and get a confirmation, when in reality nothing happened — allowing for repeat attempts as fast as Windows lets them, at five per reboot. There is no fix for this vulnerability other than replacing the SPI chip with one that doesn't contain the bug.

The team glitched two specific Winbond chip models, but they theorize the issue extends further into the maker's lineup, as the flaw allegedly lies with the RPMC engine design. Flash chips from other firms in the test were not affected to the same extent.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

As for AMD machines, the situation is both worse and better, with two related vulnerabilities. The team verified at least one of the two attacks across AMD machines from Zen 2 up to an AI 5 330 laptop. They theorize that considering the mechanisms, all contemporary AMD setups may be vulnerable, at least for standard consumer hardware using fTPM. That's multiple millions of machines potentially at risk, on the low side.

The first is simple enough. On the tested machines whose SPI flash didn't use RPMC — rollback protection — you can just make a copy of the SPI flash's contents when the counter is low, and just flash it again once you've used up your free tries. Bad enough, yes, but the second vulnerability should elicit facepalms from security architects.

According to the paper, AMD's firmware controller for non-volatile storage — the bit that talks to the SPI flash — does not verify that the failed-attempt counter increase actually took place. It'll just issue the order to +1 it and be done, opening the avenue for an attacker to simply intercept that order (again, with a cheap board) and ignore it without even needing HMAC keys, so the counter never changes.

The latter vulnerability should be fixable via a firmware update, almost certainly via AMD's AGESA software. The problem is one of practicality: in the past, updating AGESA on client hardware meant that every OEM had to create fresh BIOSes for affected machines, many of which are assuredly out of their support window.

Anyone who's lived through the Spectre and Meltdown days knows how hard it is in practice, as OEMs are exceedingly slow to publish updates, and have a distaste for providing fixes for hardware that's more than a few years old.

The researchers contacted every company involved in their tests, informing them of their findings, but sadly "none of them has committed to fixing the root-cause vulnerabilities" — at least, as of this writing, only Microsoft announced a policy change recommending users enter six-digit PINs instead of the current four during setup.

#10425. ‘It was the talk of the playground’: Google’s AI features blocked by L.A. school officials

School districts are taking steps to block Google’s artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the company gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America’s classrooms.

In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices. The move makes the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) the largest district to sideline the company, which has said it will not separate its search product from AI tools for education.

The L.A. district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA, which has pushed for screen-time limits and tech oversight in the district.

The group had several members who weighed in at a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s AI committee on Friday, November 13. By that Monday, AI Overview was gone.

“It was the talk of the playground,” Lee said.

Google is the dominant provider of education technology for America’s classrooms. Beyond its low-cost Chromebooks, the most widely used student laptops, Google’s suite of education apps like Google Docs and Classroom has become integral to classwork, homework, and communication among students and teachers.

But concerns about AI’s impact on learning have ignited a battle between schools and Google. In September, the country’s two largest school districts—in New York and L.A.—announced one-year moratoriums on student use of generative AI, and Google has said it’s not possible to take AI out of its search products. Schools are considering other internet search providers.

LAUSD said in a statement it temporarily suspended AI Overview to ensure student experiences are “age-appropriate and safe.” It also said it continually evaluates its digital safeguards, including third-party tools. It was likely using such a tool that it was able to disable AI Overview.

Schools Beyond Screens LA asked parents to send videos of what laptop screens looked like and received clips showing that AI Overview was no longer an option in Google search on district devices. Then activists reached out to the district, which confirmed AI Overview was disabled. Lee said they had no other details on how it was done or how long it is intended to stay disabled.

“We’re thrilled LAUSD did this,” said Lee. “AI is seeping into everything. It’s dangerous. It’s hurting learning. And it’s a corporate overreach into public schools. It’s Big Tech attempting to strongarm tech policy without anyone’s consent.”

Other districts, such as Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia, have developed plug-ins to remove AI summaries for students searching on Google, according to multiple published reports.

Google is increasingly at center of school tech backlash

Schools are seeing growing backlash against technology, starting with cell phones and screen time and now focusing on AI, amid concerns that students are using AI to think for them.

The Mountain View, California-based company in August found itself at the center of controversy. That’s when it said it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. Weeks later, New York City and L.A. schools banned generative AI. In New York, the ban applies to all elementary and middle school students, and in Los Angeles all students K-12 are banned from using AI on school devices. Both districts said the ban would allow officials to develop AI policies this academic year.

Then, in early November, Google backtracked. It published a blog post saying it would instead turn off Gemini and all search tools by default for K-12 schools in the coming months. Administrators would have to turn on each tool if they wanted students to access them.

Google said this was to give schools more choice. But the choice to turn off AI altogether is not there.

While the blog post does not explicitly say search can’t be used without AI, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times: “Search and AI are deeply integrated.” If schools ban AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The integration of AI in search isn’t new. Google introduced AI Overview in 2025, and anyone who uses Google search will get AI answers to many search results. Google insists AI Overview is an integral part of its search product now and cannot be separated.

Earlier this month, hundreds of Google employees signed a petition asking the company’s leadership to allow schools to turn off AI features “without disrupting their ability to use search as a whole.”

“The way the decision has been reported in the press is poor, and makes Google, and our Education and Search products as a result, look like we’re punishing schools for not using AI,” the petition said. “Many students, educators and parents have concerns about AI in the classroom, as is shown by many school districts who have placed moratoriums or bans on such technology. It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products.”

Google has made some changes—but not enough, activists say

Google says it hears parents’ and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to “shortcut learning” and that it shares the same goal: helping students learn. But what many parents and teachers want—the ability to bypass AI entirely and allow students to use Google search like it was in, say, 2024—is not something Google offers. This has forced districts across the U.S. to choose between restricting students’ access to AI and maintaining access to the popular search engine.

Instead of offering an AI-free search product for schools, Google announced a pilot “guided learning” tool that walks students “step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers.”

“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” the company said in a statement.

Currently, Google search offers AI Overview, which contains summarized answers resulting from general searches, and AI Mode, which is a chatbot interaction. Guided learning, which is not yet available, will walk users through steps intended to support critical thinking to get to the answer.

L.A. schools had already disabled Google’s AI Mode at the beginning of the school year on school-issued student devices, said Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, during a school board committee meeting on artificial intelligence last week. Educators and staff still have access.

“We understand this as a deeper embedding of AI into the education suite,” Kelanic said. He added, to applause, that the district is not bound to Google’s products if officials determine the changes are not in line with the district’s priorities.

“We have choices,” Kelanic said. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight.”

—Barbara Ortutay, Jocelyn Gecker and Cheyanne Mumphrey, Associated Press

#10422. Travis and Jason Kelce’s Garage Beer lands $20 million as craft brewers pull back

Travis Kelce’s beer brand just secured a huge financial deal to help promote its popular brew. On Tuesday, Travis and his brother Jason Kelce’s Garage Beer brand secured a $20 million revolving credit from Tiger Finance, according to a release. 

The funding comes at a time when the independent beer industry has been facing many challenges. The rise in operation costs, slowing business openings, and declines in sales have forced many breweries to close down or refinance. But this celebrity-backed brand is only seeing success. 

Andy Cerussi, the senior managing director of Tiger Finance, said in the release that the company is thrilled to have been chosen as the preferred financial partner, saying that the company is “impressed with [the] impact the Kelce brothers have had on positively influencing brand awareness.”

Brian Amicon, president of Garage Beer, told Inc. that as the company continues to grow, this financing allows it greater flexibility. 

“From strengthening our distribution to investing in the brand and creating more opportunities to connect with consumers, it puts us in a strong position to keep building what we’ve started,” Amicon said. “We’re proud of the progress we’ve made and excited to keep pushing forward.”

A $20 million bet on Garage Beer’s brand strength

The debt deal allows Garage Beer to expand its product line and enter new markets. At $20 million, the financing sits on the smaller side of the funding spectrum—in the bottom quarter of deals tracked, according to Deal Room. But for a consumer company like a beer line, debt against brand strength gives growth capital without diluting equity. This revolving line will give Garage Beer flexible access to capital tied to its brand value.

The Columbus, Ohio-based brand originally launched as a local craft light lager by Braxton Brewing Co., but was spun off into an independent company in 2023 by its CEO, Andy Sauer. According to VinePair, the Kelce brothers joined Garage Beer in the summer of 2024 by acquiring a majority stake and becoming co-owners and operators. This move rapidly boosted the brand’s national visibility. In late 2025, Durational Capital Management announced its strategic investment partnership with the company. 

A cofounder of Durational Capital said in the release that the company appreciates Tiger’s creativity and partnership “to structure a credit facility that leverages the strength of Garage Beer’s brand to support the company’s growth objectives.”

Garage Beer is expanding while competitors retrench

Neil Reid, a professor at the University of Toledo who studies the craft beer industry, told Inc. that the brand’s trajectory stands out.

“Garage Beer’s aggressive expansion is highly unusual in today’s beer market,” Reid said. 

He noted that the company has expanded distribution to all 50 states and added more than 100,000 barrels of volume in 2025, reportedly the largest increase among U.S. craft brewers. 

“Rather than retrenching, Garage Beer is using the downturn to gain market share from competitors,” Reid told Inc.

He added that brands with the capacity for growth through distribution often tend to be a simple product and have broad appeal, sales momentum, enough capital to fund expansion, name recognition, and scalable operations. Brands like small craft breweries that rely on taprooms and direct sales struggle with reaching that same momentum. Even if they have strong local followings, having fewer financial resources and less distributor support can be a challenge.

“By offering a simple, familiar product rather than a niche craft beer, the brand can attract a larger audience, generate stronger retail turnover, and expand more easily across geographic markets,” Reid said.

But he cautioned against treating Garage Beer as a model for the rest of the industry, noting, “The brand benefits from factors that most breweries lack, including celebrity backing, substantial capital, extensive marketing reach, and a highly scalable business model. Differentiation remains important, but differentiation alone is rarely sufficient.”

Celebrity attention still has to translate into repeat sales

Claudia Kubowicz Malhotra, marketing professor at the University of North Carolina’s Kenan-Flagler Business School, told Inc. that celebrity attention is only the first step.

“To continue to build the brand, awareness needs to translate to interest, desire, and action,” Kubowicz Malhotra said. “Consumers need to look and ask for the beer by name. Ultimately, this needs to translate to sales.”

As Garage Beer adds new products, she said, it can grow successfully “if new product offerings reinforce the brand positioning—a light beer that tastes like beer.”

To judge whether the brand has staying power, Kubowicz Malhotra told Inc. she would look beyond sales: “I would also look for customer retention and repurchase behavior as well as word of mouth.”

Tiger Finance and Durational Capital Management did not immediately respond to Inc.’s request for comment.

—Lucia Auerbach

This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com.
